title: Returning a Value
description: Methods that work something out and hand the answer back.

items: A printed value is shown once. You cannot add to it, compare it or save it.
A method that **returns** its result hands back a value you can do anything with.
Two changes: swap `void` for the type you hand back, and use `return` to hand it back.

parts.label: modifier
parts.note: Needed for methods beside `main`, as before.

parts.label: return type
parts.note: A promise: this method hands back an `int`.

parts.label: name
parts.note: What you write to call it.

parts.label: parameters
parts.note: Two ints come in, each with its own type.

steps.note: To work out the right side of `=`, Java must call `add`. It jumps in.
The parameters arrive with the arguments.
`a + b` is 7. `return` hands 7 back and leaves the method.
The call is replaced by 7, exactly as if you had typed `7`. `a` and `b` are gone.
`add(10, 5)` runs and becomes 15, used straight away.

content.title: Watch the value come back
content.outro: A returned value can be stored, printed or used in a bigger calculation. By the time the rest of the line runs, it is just a value.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `twice(4)` hands back 8, so the line becomes `8 + 1`, which is 9.

items: `return` does two jobs: hands the value back, and **finishes** the method there and then.
Code straight after a `return` can never run. javac calls it unreachable and refuses to compile.
Leaving early is handy: deal with special cases first, with no `else` needed.

steps.note: Hand back `"A"` and leave. The lines below never run this time.
The call became `"A"`, so it prints.
Print it. Three returns in the method, exactly one taken each time.

content.title: Watch return leave early
content.outro: No `else` anywhere: once a `return` runs, nothing below it can. Try `grade(12)` and it reaches `return "Fail"`.

items.title: missing return statement
items.text: Below 40 there is no `return`. The error points at the closing brace: the spot reached with nothing to hand back.

items.title: Compiles
items.text: Every route through the method ends in a `return`.

content.title: Every path must return
content.caption: Java refuses to let a gap through, the same reasoning as the `variable might not have been initialized` error from Module 4. Fix: a final `return` outside every `if`, or finish the chain with `else`.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: 50 makes the `if` true, so it returns `"big"`. 5 skips the `if` and reaches `return "small"`.

items: A method can return a `boolean`. That lets you give a test a name.
Then the call reads like English: `if (canVote(age))`.

content.caption: `isEven` has no `if`: `n % 2 == 0` already **is** true or false, so return it directly.

items: Returns plus the loops from Module 5 make a toolbox. Each method does one job and hands back one answer.
`digitSum` and `reverse` divide `n` down to nothing. That is safe: `n` is their own copy, so the caller's number is untouched.
These four methods plus a menu are this module's project. You have already written the hard part.

content.caption: Each method can be tested on its own, with one line in `main`.

items.title: int: returns

content.title: Printing is not returning
content.caption: Let the method work out the answer and `return` it. The caller then decides: print it, save it, or use it in a calculation.
A `void` method can use `return;` with no value. It just means "I am finished", like `break` for a whole method. A guard at the top deals with bad input first, so the rest can trust it.

content.value: One method, one job, one thing returned. Wanting to hand back two values means you need two methods or, from Module 8, an object.
content.title: One job each

content.question: Which header promises to hand back a whole number?
content.explain: The return type sits between `static` and the name. `int` promises a whole number; `void` promises nothing.

practice.question: Write square(int n) that returns n times n, then use a loop in main to print the squares of 1 to 5.
Write largest(int a, int b) that returns the bigger of the two. A ternary makes it one line.
Write isValidScore(int score) that returns true only for 0 to 100, then use it in an if to accept or reject a number.
This does not compile with `missing return statement`. Fix it so every possible age gets an answer.

quiz.question: What do you change to make a method hand a value back?
options: Replace void with the type of the value, and use return
Just add a return at the end
quiz.explain: The return type is the promise and `return` keeps it. Java will not let the two disagree.

quiz.question: What does `return` do besides handing back a value?
options: It ends the method immediately, so nothing below it runs
quiz.explain: That is why early returns need no `else`, and why code written after a return will not compile.

quiz.question: Why does this fail: `static String grade(int m) { if (m >= 40) { return "Pass"; } }`?
options: A mark below 40 reaches the end of the method with nothing returned
String cannot be a return type
The if needs an else if
quiz.explain: `missing return statement`. Java insists that every possible route out of the method hands back a value.

quiz.question: What is the tidy way to write `isEven`?
quiz.explain: The comparison is already a boolean, so returning it directly says the same thing in one line.

quiz.question: What does a bare `return;` do in a void method?
options: Leaves the method early without handing anything back
quiz.explain: It is the method-level `break`, and it is ideal for a guard at the top that rejects impossible input.
